claim: TGFβ receptors are discretely organized to segregated spatial domains at the cell surface.
source: We find that TGFβ receptors are discretely organized to segregated spatial domains at the cell surface.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Integrin-rich focal adhesions organize TβRII around TβRI.
source: Integrin-rich focal adhesions organize TβRII around TβRI, limiting the integration of TβRII while sequestering TβRI at these sites.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by TIRF imaging and colocalization analysis.

claim: Focal adhesions limit the integration of TβRII while sequestering TβRI at these sites.
source: Integrin-rich focal adhesions organize TβRII around TβRI, limiting the integration of TβRII while sequestering TβRI at these sites.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing TβRII exclusion and TβRI enrichment at focal adhesions.

claim: Disruption of cellular tension leads to a collapse of TGFβ receptor spatial organization.
source: Disruption of cellular tension leads to a collapse of this spatial organization and drives formation of heteromeric TβRI/TβRII complexes and Smad activation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments using Y27632 and blebbistatin to disrupt tension.

claim: Disruption of cellular tension drives formation of heteromeric TβRI/TβRII complexes.
source: Disruption of cellular tension leads to a collapse of this spatial organization and drives formation of heteromeric TβRI/TβRII complexes and Smad activation.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing increased TβRI/TβRII complex formation after ROCK inhibition.

claim: Disruption of cellular tension drives Smad activation.
source: Disruption of cellular tension leads to a collapse of this spatial organization and drives formation of heteromeric TβRI/TβRII complexes and Smad activation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased Smad3 phosphorylation on compliant substrates.

claim: TGFβ signals through a heterotetrameric complex of transmembrane receptor kinases.
source: TGFβ signals through a heterotetrameric complex of transmembrane receptor kinases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TGFβ signaling cited in the introduction.

claim: Once the TGFβ ligand is activated from its latent form, it binds directly to a dimer of type II receptors (TβRII).
source: Once the TGFβ ligand is activated from its latent form, it binds directly to a dimer of type II receptors (TβRII) (Annes, 2003; Munger et al., 1999; Wipff et al., 2007; Munger and Sheppard, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The ligand-bound TβRII complex recruits and phosphorylates two type I receptors (TβRI) – either Alk5 or Alk1.
source: The ligand-bound TβRII complex recruits and phosphorylates two type I receptors (TβRI) – either Alk5 or Alk1 (Wrana et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: TβRI phosphorylates and activates canonical Smad proteins and multiple non-canonical effectors, such as RhoA, TAK1 and Akt.
source: TβRI, in turn, phosphorylates and activates canonical Smad proteins and multiple non-canonical effectors, such as RhoA, TAK1 and Akt (Massague, 1998; Feng and Derynck, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Recruitment of Alk5 to the TβRII complex stimulates phosphorylation of Smad2/3.
source: Specifically, recruitment of Alk5 to the TβRII complex stimulates phosphorylation of Smad2/3, whereas Alk1 recruitment drives activation of Smad1/5/8 (Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Alk1 recruitment drives activation of Smad1/5/8.
source: Specifically, recruitment of Alk5 to the TβRII complex stimulates phosphorylation of Smad2/3, whereas Alk1 recruitment drives activation of Smad1/5/8 (Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The inappropriate shift of TβRII multimerization partner from Alk5 to Alk1 underlies disease processes ranging from vascular disorders to osteoarthritis.
source: The inappropriate shift of TβRII multimerization partner from Alk5 to Alk1 underlies disease processes ranging from vascular disorders to osteoarthritis (Blaney Davidson et al., 2009; Goumans, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TGFβ receptors associate with integrins.
source: Not only do TGFβ receptors associate with one another, but also with a number of other receptor families, notably integrins (Scaffidi et al., 2004; Garamszegi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Integrin α2β1 physically interacts with TGFβ receptors and is involved in collagen-induced Smad phosphorylation.
source: Garamszegi et al. revealed a physical interaction between integrin α2β1 and TGFβ receptors involved in collagen-induced Smad phosphorylation (Garamszegi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Upon integrin binding to the extracellular matrix, the formation of focal adhesions stimulates actomyosin contractility to generate cellular tension.
source: Upon integrin binding to the extracellular matrix, the formation of focal adhesions stimulates actomyosin contractility to generate cellular tension (DuFort et al., 2011; Giancotti, 1999; Ingber, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Through a Rho/ROCK-dependent mechanism, cells establish tensional homeostasis with the physical features of the extracellular environment.
source: Through this Rho/ROCK-dependent mechanism, cells establish tensional homeostasis with the physical features of the extracellular environment (DuFort et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cellular tension can amplify, alter, or suppress cellular responses to growth factor signaling.
source: Cellular tension can amplify, alter, or suppress cellular responses to growth factor signaling (Allen et al., 2012; McBeath et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The functional state of β-catenin, YAP/TAZ, and MAPK is modulated by cellular tension.
source: The functional state of many intracellular effectors, including β-catenin, YAP/TAZ, and MAPK, is modulated by cellular tension (Samuel et al., 2011; Dupont et al., 2011; Wang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The activation of latent TGFβ ligand is regulated by cellular tension in a Rho/ROCK-dependent manner.
source: The activation of latent TGFβ ligand, as well as the phosphorylation, nuclear translocation and transactivation of Smads is regulated by cellular tension in a Rho/ROCK-dependent manner (Allen et al., 2012; Wipff and Hinz, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The phosphorylation, nuclear translocation and transactivation of Smads is regulated by cellular tension in a Rho/ROCK-dependent manner.
source: The activation of latent TGFβ ligand, as well as the phosphorylation, nuclear translocation and transactivation of Smads is regulated by cellular tension in a Rho/ROCK-dependent manner (Allen et al., 2012; Wipff and Hinz, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Immunofluorescence of TβRII in both wildtype and transfected ATDC5 cells yielded similar results, revealing specific punctate staining.
source: Immunofluorescence of TβRII in both wildtype and transfected ATDC5 cells yielded similar results, revealing specific punctate staining that did not provide structural information (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spinning disc confocal microscopy of TβRII-mEmerald revealed shadowed regions where TβRII expression is completely absent.
source: Spinning disc confocal microscopy of TβRII-mEmerald allowed visualization of its spatial organization, revealing shadowed regions where TβRII expression is completely absent (indicated by arrows, Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: TIRF microscopy revealed segregated domains of TβRII and TβRI.
source: Switching from widefield microscopy (Figure 1E) to TIRF on the same cell vividly revealed segregated domains of TβRII (Figure 1F) and TβRI (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 1E-H.

claim: The sequestration of TβRII from TβRI was present with either the canonical (Alk5) or non-canonical (Alk1) type I TGFβ receptors.
source: The sequestration of TβRII from TβRI was present with either the canonical (Alk5) or non-canonical (Alk1) type I TGFβ receptors (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: When co-expressed in the same cell, TβRII is enriched at the boundary of discrete TβRI domains.
source: Indeed, when co-expressed in the same cell, TβRII is enriched at the boundary of discrete TβRI domains, demonstrating a novel spatial segregation of these signaling partners (Figure 1I–L).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1I-L.

claim: Individual TβRI and TβRII receptors showed a range of mobility, resulting in groups of immobile, confined, or freely diffusive receptors.
source: For both TβRI and TβRII, individual receptors showed a range of mobility, resulting in groups of immobile, confined, or freely diffusive receptors (representative tracks, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by sptPALM data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mobility of each group of TβRI did not differ significantly from TβRII.
source: Mobility of each group of TβRI did not differ significantly from TβRII (Figure 2E), but the diffusion coefficient of TβRI was slightly higher (Figure 2F), perhaps because of its lower molecular weight (TβRI/Alk5 56 kDa vs. TβRII 65 kDa).
evidence: This is supported by sptPALM data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of TβRI was slightly higher than TβRII, perhaps because of its lower molecular weight (TβRI/Alk5 56 kDa vs. TβRII 65 kDa).
source: Mobility of each group of TβRI did not differ significantly from TβRII (Figure 2E), but the diffusion coefficient of TβRI was slightly higher (Figure 2F), perhaps because of its lower molecular weight (TβRI/Alk5 56 kDa vs. TβRII 65 kDa).
evidence: This is supported by sptPALM data shown in Figure 2F and includes speculation about the mechanism.

claim: TβRI and TβRII are significantly less mobile in cellular domains enriched with clusters of spatially organized receptors.
source: Relative to whole cell TGFβ receptor dynamics, TβRI and TβRII are significantly less mobile in cellular domains enriched with clusters of spatially organized receptors (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by sptPALM data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The spatially organized population of TGFβ receptors is slower and more confined, possibly due to interactions with other proteins.
source: Thus, this spatially organized population of TGFβ receptors is slower and more confined, possibly due to interactions with other proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mobility data, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: TβRII is absent from sites of adhesions and forms a peripheral ring surrounding integrin α2.
source: Specifically, TβRII is absent from sites of adhesions and forms a peripheral ring surrounding integrin α2, resulting in distinct patterns of spatial localization (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TβRII spatial organization is absent in cells grown on poly-l-lysine-coated substrates that facilitate integrin-independent cell adhesion.
source: Interestingly, this spatial organization is absent in cells grown on poly-l-lysine-coated substrates that facilitate integrin-independent cell adhesion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TβRII organization at sites of adhesion is dependent upon integrin activity.
source: Therefore, TβRII organization at sites of adhesion is dependent upon integrin activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TβRII organization is absent on poly-l-lysine substrates.

claim: TβRI (Alk5 and Alk1) is precisely colocalized with integrin α2 within focal adhesions.
source: TβRI (Alk5 and Alk1) is precisely colocalized with integrin α2 within focal adhesions, such that adhesions appear yellow (Figure 3B,C) and regression line slopes (Figure 3Bi,Ci) are higher relative to TβRII (Figure 3A,Ai).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF imaging and colocalization analysis shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Integrin α2 colocalizes significantly more with Alk5 and Alk1 than with TβRII.
source: This analysis reveals that integrin α2 colocalizes significantly more with Alk5 and Alk1 than with TβRII (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The specific localization of TβRII near focal adhesions is apparent in cells of both mesenchymal (ATDC5, Saos-2) and epithelial (MCF10A) origin.
source: The specific localization of TβRII near focal adhesions is apparent in cells of both mesenchymal (ATDC5, Figure 3A–C,E; Saos-2, Figure 3F) and epithelial (MCF10A, Figure 3G) origin and is observed whether integrin α2 or integrin αV is tagged with a fluorescent protein (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A-G.

claim: The overall spatial organization of TGFβ receptors at sites of adhesion is not affected upon stimulation with exogenous TGFβ.
source: The overall spatial organization of TGFβ receptors at sites of adhesion is not affected upon stimulation with exogenous TGFβ (Figure 3I), suggesting that this spatiotemporal organization is regulated through mechanisms independent from TGFβ ligand addition.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The spatiotemporal organization of TGFβ receptors is regulated through mechanisms independent from TGFβ ligand addition.
source: The overall spatial organization of TGFβ receptors at sites of adhesion is not affected upon stimulation with exogenous TGFβ (Figure 3I), suggesting that this spatiotemporal organization is regulated through mechanisms independent from TGFβ ligand addition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TGFβ stimulation does not affect receptor organization.

claim: TβRI is preferentially enriched and TβRII is preferentially excluded at sites of adhesion.
source: SptPALM shows, both qualitatively and quantitatively, that TβRI is preferentially enriched and TβRII is preferentially excluded at sites of adhesion (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by sptPALM data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: TβRII 'bounces' around the edges of individual focal adhesions but is rarely incorporated within the focal adhesion.
source: Analysis of individual TβRII trajectories shows that TβRII 'bounces' around the edges of individual focal adhesions (Figure 4E) but is rarely incorporated within the focal adhesion, as is common for TβRI (Figure 4D,i–ii).
evidence: This is supported by sptPALM trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: TβRII mobility is confined near focal adhesions, which sequester and immobilize TβRI.
source: Trajectory maps reveal that TβRII mobility is confined near focal adhesions, which sequester and immobilize TβRI (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is supported by sptPALM trajectory maps shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: A higher fraction of immobilized TβRI is present inside adhesions relative to outside.
source: Indeed, a higher fraction of immobilized TβRI is present inside adhesions relative to outside (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by sptPALM data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The diffusion coefficient for TβRI decreases for tracks inside adhesions compared to those outside.
source: Accordingly, the diffusion coefficient for TβRI decreases for tracks inside adhesions compared to those outside, demonstrating that this spatial organization specifically limits TβRI mobility (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by sptPALM data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Mass spectrometric analysis of proteins that precipitate with Flag-tagged TβRI (Alk5) and TβRII revealed hundreds of proteins, several of which were specifically enriched compared with precipitates of untransfected (mock) cells.
source: Mass spectrometric analysis of proteins that precipitate with Flag-tagged TβRI (Alk5) and TβRII revealed hundreds of proteins, several of which were specifically enriched compared with precipitates of untransfected (mock) cells.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: The mass spectrometry analysis identified proteins already known to interact with TβRs, such as PRMT5 and PRMT1.
source: The analysis identified proteins already known to interact with TβRs, such as PRMT5 and PRMT1 (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data and citation to prior work.

claim: TβRs precipitated integrin αV and endogenous cofilin.
source: TβRs also precipitated several adhesion-related proteins, including integrin αV and endogenous cofilin, as shown in the annotated spectra (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Integrin αV associates with both TβRI and TβRII.
source: The peptide counts (graph insets) indicate that integrin αV associates with both TβRI and TβRII, and that cofilin preferentially associates with TβRII (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry peptide counts shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Cofilin preferentially associates with TβRII.
source: The peptide counts (graph insets) indicate that integrin αV associates with both TβRI and TβRII, and that cofilin preferentially associates with TβRII (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry peptide counts shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Cofilin is an actin-binding protein that severs ADP-actin filaments at the leading edge of migratory cells.
source: Cofilin is an actin-binding protein that severs ADP-actin filaments at the leading edge of migratory cells (Pollard and Borisy, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Previous reports implicate cofilin as a target of TGFβ-activated RhoA, which promotes actin reorganization through ROCK, LIMK and cofilin.
source: Previous reports implicate cofilin as a target of TGFβ-activated RhoA, which promotes actin reorganization through ROCK, LIMK and cofilin (Vardouli et al., 2005; Lamouille et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: This is the first report of a complex between TGFβ receptors and cofilin.
source: However, this is the first report, to our knowledge, of a complex between TGFβ receptors and cofilin.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation confirmed that integrin αV forms a complex with both TβRI and TβRII.
source: To confirm these mass spectrometry findings, we performed co-immunoprecipitation on cells expressing Flag-tagged TβRI/II and tagged integrin αV or cofilin (Figure 5C,D). Consistent with the mass spectrometry peptide counts, integrin αV forms a complex with both TβRI and TβRII, whereas cofilin primarily interacts with TβRII.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Cofilin primarily interacts with TβRII.
source: Consistent with the mass spectrometry peptide counts, integrin αV forms a complex with both TβRI and TβRII, whereas cofilin primarily interacts with TβRII.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Within 15 min of adding Y27632 or blebbistatin, the peripheral ring of TβRII completely collapses.
source: Within 15 min of adding Y27632 (Figure 6A,B) or blebbistatin (Figure 6C,D), the peripheral ring of TβRII completely collapses.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: The segregation of TβRII from TβRI and integrin α2 at sites of adhesion is dynamically released upon ROCK or myosin II inhibition.
source: The segregation of TβRII from TβRI and integrin α2 at sites of adhesion is dynamically released, such that TβRII (Video 1) converges and colocalizes with integrin α2 (Video 2, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Videos 1-3.

claim: TβRII is significantly more colocalized with integrin α2 after addition of Y27632 and blebbistatin.
source: Quantitative analysis demonstrates that TβRII is significantly more colocalized with integrin α2 after addition of Y27632 and blebbistatin (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Disruption of tension with Y27632 enhances integrin αV association with TβRI but reduces its association with TβRII.
source: We find that cellular tension not only regulates the spatial organization of integrins and TGFβ receptors, but also affects their physical associations with each other; though these interactions may be direct or indirect. Specifically, while disruption of tension with the ROCK inhibitor enhanced integrin αV association with TβRI, it almost completely blocked the association between integrin αV and TβRII (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: ROCK-inhibition stimulates formation of heteromeric TβRI/TβRII complexes.
source: Release of this discrete spatial segregation of TGFβ receptors at focal adhesions allows the receptor subunits to interact such that ROCK-inhibition stimulates formation of heteromeric TβRI/TβRII complexes (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A reduction in cellular tension through culture on compliant substrates significantly drives TβRI/TβRII complex formation.
source: To examine the effect of manipulating cellular tension under physiological conditions, we cultured cells on polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) substrates of varying stiffness. A reduction in cellular tension through culture on compliant substrates significantly drives TβRI/TβRII complex formation (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Culturing cells on compliant substrates leads to significantly increased endogenous Smad3 phosphorylation.
source: To determine the effect of tension-sensitive TβR localization and heteromerization on downstream TGFβ effectors, we evaluated the phosphorylation of Smad3. Culturing cells on compliant substrates leads to significantly increased endogenous Smad3 phosphorylation (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The effect of TGFβ on Smad3 phosphorylation is substrate-dependent, such that TGFβ induces Smad3 phosphorylation on 0.5 kPa substrates but not on 16 kPa substrates.
source: Interestingly, the effect of TGFβ on Smad3 phosphorylation is substrate-dependent, such that TGFβ induces Smad3 phosphorylation on 0.5 kPa substrates but not on 16 kPa substrates (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The spatial organization of TβRI and TβRII by integrins at focal adhesions affords tension-sensitive control of TβRI and TβRII multimerization and activation of Smad3.
source: Thus the spatial organization of TβRI and TβRII by integrins at focal adhesions affords tension-sensitive control of TβRI and TβRII multimerization and activation of Smad3, providing a mechanosensitive mechanism by which cells calibrate their response to TGFβ.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cellular tension regulates TGFβ receptor spatial organization and interactions at focal adhesions.
source: Here we show that cellular tension regulates TGFβ receptor spatial organization and interactions at focal adhesions, providing a novel mechanism for the cellular integration of signaling by physical and biochemical cues.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the manuscript.

claim: Single particle tracking reveals the dynamics of individual TGFβ receptor molecules, and identifies populations of TGFβ receptors with distinct behaviors and mobility near and far from sites of focal adhesions.
source: Single particle tracking reveals the dynamics of individual TGFβ receptor molecules, and identifies populations of TGFβ receptors with distinct behaviors and mobility near and far from sites of focal adhesions.
evidence: This is supported by sptPALM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The confined population of TGFβ receptors at focal adhesions has lower mobility than the freely diffusive receptor population far from sites of adhesion.
source: The confined population of TGFβ receptors at focal adhesions has lower mobility than the freely diffusive receptor population far from sites of adhesion.
evidence: This is supported by sptPALM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: This novel spatial organization of TβRI and TβRII at sites of adhesion provides mechanosensitive control of TGFβ receptor multimerization and function independently of TGFβ ligand stimulation.
source: This novel spatial organization of TβRI and TβRII at sites of adhesion provides mechanosensitive control of TGFβ receptor multimerization and function independently of TGFβ ligand stimulation.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is potential for two differentially regulated populations of TGFβ receptors – one that is TGFβ-sensitive and one that is tension-sensitive.
source: Overall, this reveals the potential of two differentially regulated populations of TGFβ receptors – one that is TGFβ-sensitive and one that is tension-sensitive – a finding that may contribute to the context-dependent signaling outcomes of this pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Integrins activate TGFβ from its latent form through cellular tension generated by actomyosin contraction.
source: At the level of the TGFβ ligand, integrins activate TGFβ from its latent form through cellular tension generated by actomyosin contraction (Wipff et al., 2007; Munger and Sheppard, 2011; Wells and Discher, 2008; Giacomini et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The recruitment of TGFβ receptors to focal adhesions would enrich their access to integrin-activated TGFβ.
source: The observed recruitment of TGFβ receptors to focal adhesions would enrich their access to this reservoir of integrin-activated TGFβ.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications of the findings.

claim: Focal adhesions may sequester TβRI from TβRII to limit their activity in the presence of ligand.
source: At the receptor level, focal adhesions may sequester TβRI from TβRII to limit their activity in the presence of ligand.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications of the findings.

claim: Focal adhesions may create structured TβRI and TβRII boundaries that prime a robust response when cells encounter the correct combination of physical and biochemical cues.
source: Alternatively, focal adhesions may create structured TβRI and TβRII boundaries that prime a robust response when cells encounter the correct combination of physical and biochemical cues.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications of the findings.

claim: Chondrocytes grown in TGFβ on 0.5 MPa substrates induce differentiation markers far beyond levels induced by either cue alone.
source: In addition, chondrocytes grown in TGFβ on 0.5 MPa substrates induce differentiation markers far beyond levels induced by either cue alone (Allen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The effect of substrate stiffness or cellular tension/Rho/ROCK activity on downstream TGFβ signaling is synergistic and nonlinear.
source: We and others have reported that the effect of substrate stiffness or cellular tension/Rho/ROCK activity on downstream TGFβ signaling is synergistic and nonlinear (Allen et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012; Leight et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The newly described regulation of TGFβ receptor multimerization and downstream signaling may couple the mechanosensitive activity of the TGFβ pathway to physical cues.
source: The mechanisms responsible for such synergy have been unclear, but this newly described regulation of TGFβ receptor multimerization and downstream signaling may couple the mechanosensitive activity of the TGFβ pathway to physical cues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Cellular tension impacts the activation, translocation, and function of intracellular effectors including small GTP-ases, kinases and transcriptional regulators such as Smads and YAP/TAZ.
source: Cellular tension impacts the activation, translocation, and function of intracellular effectors including small GTP-ases, kinases and transcriptional regulators such as Smads and YAP/TAZ (Allen et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012; Dupont et al., 2011; Leight et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Known mechanisms are insufficient to explain the ability of physical cues to modulate cell-type specific responses to BMP, EGF, and other growth factors.
source: However, known mechanisms are insufficient to explain the ability of physical cues to modulate cell-type specific responses to BMP, EGF, and other growth factors (Wang et al., 2012; Paszek et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: EGF receptor binds actin and colocalizes with integrin α2β1.
source: EGF receptor binds actin and colocalizes with integrin α2β1 (Alam et al., 2007), while the receptor CD44 interacts with several components of the focal adhesion complex, such that hyaluronan-bound CD44 activates c-Src and Rac1 (Turley et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The receptor CD44 interacts with several components of the focal adhesion complex, such that hyaluronan-bound CD44 activates c-Src and Rac1.
source: EGF receptor binds actin and colocalizes with integrin α2β1 (Alam et al., 2007), while the receptor CD44 interacts with several components of the focal adhesion complex, such that hyaluronan-bound CD44 activates c-Src and Rac1 (Turley et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Others have postulated receptor multimerization as a mechanism for mechanocoupling of TGFβ, ephrin, and T cell receptor signaling.
source: Nonetheless, others have postulated receptor multimerization as a mechanism for mechanocoupling of TGFβ, ephrin, and T cell receptor signaling (Hartman and Groves, 2011; Hynes, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In T cell receptor and ephrin signaling, the solid state is provided by ligands on the neighboring cell, which create geometric constraints that mechanically trap receptors to induce clustering.
source: In T cell receptor and ephrin signaling, the solid state is provided by ligands on the neighboring cell, which create geometric constraints that mechanically trap receptors to induce clustering (Bethani et al., 2010; Salaita et al., 2010; Hartman and Groves, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: For growth factors like TGFβ, BMP, and EGF, the ECM serves as the solid state.
source: For growth factors like TGFβ, BMP, and EGF, the ECM serves as the solid state (Hynes, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ECM proteins such as collagen II bind both TGFβ and integrin α2β1.
source: ECM proteins such as collagen II bind both TGFβ and integrin α2β1 (Zhu, 1999), imposing geometric constraints that may structure receptor clusters.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Growth factor receptor multimerization at focal adhesions, controlled by receptor interactions with integrins and with solid state growth factors, provide focal adhesions with the capability to integrate signaling between physical and biochemical cues.
source: Therefore, growth factor receptor multimerization at focal adhesions, controlled by receptor interactions with integrins and with solid state growth factors, provide focal adhesions with the capability to integrate signaling between physical and biochemical cues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and prior work.

claim: Focal adhesions segregate TβRI from TβRII in both epithelial and mesenchymal cell lineages.
source: We find that focal adhesions segregate TβRI from TβRII in both epithelial and mesenchymal cell lineages, opening the possibility that this is a general cellular mechanism for the control of TGFβ signaling.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data from multiple cell types.

claim: On stiff substrates, TGFβ preferentially activates PI3K to induce EMT instead of apoptosis.
source: On stiff substrates, TGFβ preferentially activates PI3K to induce EMT instead of apoptosis (Leight et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In osteoarthritis, the material properties of the cartilage ECM deteriorate as chondrocytes inappropriately shift the balance from canonical (Alk5/Smad2/3) to non-canonical (Alk1/Smad1/5/8) TβRI signaling.
source: In osteoarthritis, the material properties of the cartilage ECM deteriorate as chondrocytes inappropriately shift the balance from canonical (Alk5/Smad2/3) to non-canonical (Alk1/Smad1/5/8) TβRI signaling (Blaney Davidson et al., 2009).

claim: Applied physical cues, such as compression or shear flow, regulate TGFβ signaling in cartilage, vasculature, and other tissues.
